title: Buddhist Practice on Western Ground
speaker: Shuko Edie Norton
summary: The talk highlights the importance of considering cultural differences when approaching Buddhist teachings, particularly in how individualism versus collectivism shape our understanding of concepts like self and ego. This is crucial for Westerners who may be accustomed to a more individualistic approach to personal growth, as opposed to the interdependent nature of Eastern cultures. By acknowledging these cultural nuances, practitioners can gain a deeper understanding of Buddhist teachings on emptiness, attachment, and the practice of selflessness, ultimately allowing them to apply these principles in a more meaningful way.

sentences.text: The Dharma Talks we're giving this season are supposed to be about compassion, and this one actually isn't about compassion, but it's compassionate because I'm not going to talk about politics.
Your only chance.
I'm going to give a book report on this book that I read recently, which I found very interesting.
It's called Buddhist Practice on Western Ground, by a fellow named Harvey Aronson.
Because Buddhist teachings arose from Asian cultural values and languages, they can be confusing to Westerners, to Americans.
There's a chance we can even completely misunderstand some parts of these teachings.
Asian cultures emphasize values that are very different from Western culture values.
Asians emphasize respect and responsibility to the whole, the family, the ancestors, the community, and they emphasize the role one plays in the whole.
Western culture is not so concerned with responsibility to the community.
Instead, it emphasizes the individual right to do whatever we want, not what our role requires of us.
Asian cultures assume and value interrelationship, interdependence, interconnection.
We know this from Buddhist teachings.
You know the Japanese adage also: the nail that sticks up will be hammered down.
This reflects the cultural value in Japan of submerging the individual into the group.
Americans, in contrast, want to stand out.
We assume and value our independence, autonomy, and individual achievement.
About 25 years ago, I taught English in Japan at a women's university.
In one class, I had a student who came to all the classes but never did any of the homework.
At the semester's end, she came to the final and I told her she couldn't take the final because she hadn't done any of the classwork.
I thought it would be unfair to other students who had come and done the work the whole time.
She got very upset and went immediately to the program director, who came running to me very upset and said, "Oh, she must be able to take the final.
You have to let her in."
I said, "No, she can't do that.
She didn't do any of the work."
So she said, "Well, can she come back next semester if she'll agree to do the assignments?"
And I said, "Yes, she could do that."
And she did come back and she did do all the assignments.
But this was my firsthand experience of a deep cultural difference between American values and Japanese ones.
Mine was thinking of the unfairness of her behavior, her individual behavior, and she was thinking of belonging to the group, as were her superiors.
Very interesting conflict.
Cultural differences such as our individualism versus the Asian emphasis on belonging to the group can and have made it difficult for American Buddhists to understand some Buddhist teachings.

In our culture, we question authority, value familiarity with emotions, highly prize the experience of romance, appreciate the robust expression of our unique individuality, develop through free choice, and develop our relationships through verbally exchanging our thoughts, dreams, personal behavior, personal histories and feelings.
We then approach our Asian teachers, who embody the traditional cultures of Asia, where continuity of custom and reverence for those who are old and or wise is valued.
Relationships are governed by explicit and implicit rules related to the roles individuals play.
And closeness is often achieved through intuitive accommodation to others' moods.
Within these cultures, feelings and their verbal expression are not necessarily valued.
And certain feelings such as anger may even be seen as obstacles.
In these settings, spousal relationships revolve around social connections of the parents and societal obligations to produce children.
Within Buddhist culture, it is frequently taught that it is important to subordinate oneself and to practice for the sake of others.
These themes run through the teachings that we've had from American Buddhist teachers as well, because of course they were taught first by Japanese or Korean teachers.
So those themes run through our learning too.
The Buddhist teachings around self or no self and the practice of selflessness as the way to be free of suffering can be especially confusing to us.
Buddhist concepts don't fit with the American understanding of self and our belief that having a healthy ego is essential to psychological health.
Buddhism says give up self-love or self-cherishing.
Traditionally, favoring or preferring oneself or clinging to a sense of self or to things as mine can be related to pride or attachment and ultimately is to be rooted out.

Psychologically, individuals with an inclination to self-hate, as many of us Westerners have an inclination, can misunderstand calls to give up ego in the sense of self-cherishing as license for their psychological tendencies to self-recrimination.
For these individuals, there is no ground for supporting these teachings in a sensible way.
There are four common misinterpretations of the call to abandon ego in American Buddhism, or four Americans, I should say.
One of them is, we misinterpret it to mean give up self-assertion.
Psychologists in the West would distinguish between false pride and healthy self-assertion.
Traditional Asian teachers culturally may not be able to make much of a distinction easily with respect to their Western students.
Students with issues related to assertiveness may confuse it with ego and seek to give up ego, sustaining an unassertive posture in life.
One is give up ego-functioning in the technical sense.
But without ego-functioning, we could not negotiate our lives at all.
We have to have an ability to know who we are and do something and be active.
Sometimes this misunderstanding is related to the previous one, to rationalize giving up decision-making in favor of passivity.
Give up the metaphysical self.
As we have seen, it is not that we have a metaphysical self that we give up.
Rather, we just see that such a self cannot be found.
We give up clinging to or conceiving of something that is imaginary.
Is the author a practitioner or a psychologist?
He's a psychologist and he heads up a Houston Buddhist center.
I'm just going to say a little bit about him in a couple minutes here.
These are provocative descriptions, but actually ones that I have experienced myself over the years.
The traditional Asian deference to authority and family values translates in a religious context to deference toward teachers and traditions.
Knowing one's role, following the rules, despite what our initial reactions to such customs may be, this behavior may be very rewarding in a culture based on interdependence.
On the other hand, our appreciation of self-assertion is not found in cultures where group cohesion is an accepted value.

In such cultures, good feelings may be a function of good social relationships: fitting in, belonging, maintaining harmony in one's relations, occupying one's proper place, engaging in appropriate action, while at the same time regulating one's inner personal thoughts and feelings so as to ensure interdependence.
That's what I've experienced with my student who didn't do the homework.
I said no, and they said, oh, you have to keep that person in.
Those values really were in conflict in that situation.
Aaronson, as a psychotherapist and a Buddhist teacher, had his training first in Theravadan Buddhism and then later in Tibetan traditions.
One of his Tibetan teachers was Geshe Rabten, a scholar I've read and much admire.
In this book, Aaronson clarifies the difference between spiritual practice and psychology.
And psychology is, in a sense, one of our Western religions, sort of a secular religion.
He describes what each discipline, psychology and Buddhist practice, offers, and aspects of them that we Westerners can be confused by.
Both disciplines study the mind, but very, very differently.
Psychotherapy is concerned with the contents of the mind.
Psychology investigates and addresses the causes and conditions of our emotions, beliefs, and distortions of reality which create our suffering: loneliness, self-doubt, anger, envy, etc.
Psychology's purpose is to cure dysfunctional conditions and behaviors.
These are the contents of our minds.
Aaronson points out that spiritual practice, on the other hand, meditation, addresses our minds' processes of thinking these contents.
In Zazen, we observe the thoughts and feelings that come up in our minds.
We let them go and watch the next thing arise, or we notice the quality of the thoughts and feelings and observe how they change over time.
In Zazen, we train our minds to closely observe the arising and falling away of our minds' content.
Thus, we experience and realize what we think and feel is ephemeral.
It goes away.
Eventually, as we continue to observe our mind, we see that all mind content is temporary.
It doesn't last.
By training ourselves to notice and then let go of whatever comes to mind, we experience relief from suffering or dissatisfaction.
With psychotherapy, on the other hand, we endeavor to change the contents of our minds.
We probe to see if what we think and feel are true or realistic.
We try to discover the causes of our unhappiness or dysfunction.
We try to figure out how to change for the better.
Spiritual practice and psychotherapy are two distinctly different processes with different outcomes, though they can be related.
Psychotherapy can help us to uncover neuroses and fixations that may occur in Zazen while we're watching our mind.
In Zazen, we can discover neurotic fixations that we can later work on therapeutically.
But spiritual practice itself does not do psychotherapy, [unclear: "for the reason that they are"].
Spiritual practice is talking about process and psychotherapy is talking about content.
So while sitting in Zazen, we find ourselves trying to figure out what our boss was implying when he gave our co-worker the assignment that we had had before.
Or we find ourselves elaborating on what we should have said or wished we had said that morning when our partner snapped at us.
We are into the content of the mind and not the process unless we let it go and let it go again and again.
We need to just notice it, drop it, and we can continue to just watch the mind.

By training our mind to simply observe whatever comes up, not to engage it or attach to it, we eventually realize that everything is continually changing, so there is no point in clinging to feelings and thoughts.
Thus we train ourselves not to suffer.
This book delves into specific Buddhist teachings that Westerners tend to misunderstand or have confusion about.
There is the confusion around self and no self and ego due to cultural differences between Eastern and Western values.

Buddhist teaching is that when we identify with a fixed idea of self, we prevent ourselves from immediately and directly being in the present moment, which is the only way out of suffering, being in the present.

And if our fixed idea of ourselves is that we are deficient, which often is the case for us, or in some cases if our idea is that we're superior, then we stray even further from the present and suffer.
To be free of suffering, we must give up the automatic, reactive, inflexible identification with a self.
This is the task not supported by our individualistic American culture, so it can be hard to assimilate this particular teaching.
Another major confusion for us due to our culture is around anger.
The traditional Buddhist definition of anger is that anger has the intent of harming someone or something.
In Buddhist teachings, the concern about anger is not about our feeling very upset, such as how we feel about anger.
We think about our feelings and how strong they are.
It's not about us and our upset as we tend to believe.
Buddhism says anger is wrong because the expression of it is intended to harm.
We know it is not acceptable for someone practicing the Bodhisattva way to want to harm someone.
Plus, wanting to harm is an expression of clinging to ourselves, the thing that doesn't really exist.
So what is the antidote to being angry, according to Buddhist teachings?
Training the mind to be in the present, where we experience that everything is changing and there is nothing to cling to and be angry at.
Western psychology, on the contrary, focuses on and values all our emotions, even anger.
Psychology posits that angry feelings have evolved as appropriate responses to prevent intrusion on us by others, to right wrongs or to obtain something we lack.
Westerners believe anger is useful in situations where we feel our rights have been challenged or violated.
The Western perspective argues that anger is even part of what helps us in the West to develop our discrete individual selves.
That's really wildly different from Asian thought.
Yet, of course, anger does harm others if it is expressed violently or unfairly.
It does break relationships, just witness our current polarized political climate.
So as Westerners, we need to learn how to work with anger and express it non-aggressively so it can be received and can benefit our relationships.
The most fundamental skill in working spiritually with our anger is mindfulness, which allows us to know our present emotional state.
We need the ability to discern the difference between getting lost in a feeling, taken up by it, enraged, identifying with it, and actually simply observing it.
Identifying with anger causes us to feel that our very existence is threatened by the actions of another person or a situation, and that leads to wanting to harm that person or that situation.
In Zazen, we can observe our anger, become aware of it so that we can abstain from expressing it harmfully.
But to learn the causes and solutions for anger, psychology or psychotherapy is needed, so that we can examine its usually complex origins and learn to communicate differently.
Buddhist meditation was not devised to deal explicitly with pervasive interpersonal and emotional issues related to attachment difficulties.

We have a most humble and forthright illustration of this in Jack Kornfield's brutally honest report that after years in Thailand, some as a monk in retreat, quote, *my meditation had helped me very little with human relationships.
I was still tremendously immature, acting out the same painful patterns of blame and fear, acceptance and rejection that I had before my Buddhist training.
Only the horror now was that I was beginning to see these patterns more clearly.*
This is from *A Path with Heart*.
I remember reading that and thinking, oh, that's such a wonderful confession.
For Westerners, issues related to relationships, work and early family dynamics that surface as concerns in meditation are best addressed and resolved outside of traditional meditative practice.

It is hard for a teacher from a traditional culture who has no professional training to understand the coarse and subtle injuries that occurred during childhood in North America and the pressures associated with self-assertion unique to our culture.

Such teachers do not value individual feelings and their expression as we do, and therefore they do not offer us the opportunity to resolve longstanding issues in ways that Western psychology, psychotherapy, considers meaningful.
Similarly, American meditation teachers who are not therapists also lack the professional skills to address significant emotional issues that may surface, for example, during a retreat.
Meditation alone, certainly in its initial stages, in the amount that we typically do in the West, cannot be expected to heal our more intractable psychological problems.
At the same time, the skills of Buddhist meditation, when applied appropriately, can work with therapy synergistically.
Aaronson describes two ways Westerners often mishandle our anger.
First, we suppress our anger, and in fact may have been drawn to Buddhism because the teaching to abstain from anger may give us an excuse to suppress our anger.

This may lead to inauthentic relationships as well as to somatic complaints, [unclear: "which is nothing of other negative emotions"] such as hostility, resentment, depression, and anxiety that we don't know where that came from.
Or we overexpress anger through unreflective venting, which is usually loud and violent, that occurs with little forethought.
This often leads to a trail of damaged relationships.
And of course, aggression is the manifestation of the harmful intent that Buddhism warns us against.
A third concept that is different in Buddhist teachings and Western culture is attachment.
Western psychology research has found that if babies don't attach or bond with their mothers or parents, they will have trouble forming relationships as they grow up.
So in the West, psychological attachment is considered an important developmental stage.
Buddhism, however, regards attachment very differently, as an unwholesome involvement with things.
In fact, it's a variant of greed or desire, one of the three poisons that cause suffering, the other two being hatred and ignorance.

Aaronson says, quote, *Unfortunately, the oft repeated refrain about the need to give up attachment is easily confused by Westerners with giving up the objects of our desires, loved ones and loved possessions.
Because this seems so difficult to do, many individuals resist taking this teaching to heart.*
Kobun, my first teacher, used to confound his students who were suffering from jealousy about their partner by saying, "No sticky love."
I didn't know what to make of that from our Western perspective.
A fourth and final topic that he mentions that I'm going to talk about that is different in the two cultures is emptiness.
The concept is distinctly non-Western and non-materialistic, and we struggle to assimilate it.
But emptiness is the reason we are urged to give up attachment.
"All dharmas are empty," the Heart Sutra says.
Emptiness means that phenomena do not substantially exist in the solid matter in which they appear.
To experience that phenomena are not substantially established as they initially appear is to see that they are empty of inherent existence.
Their reality is only momentary in the flow of time.
And then they change, perhaps only slightly, but they do change.
And we are they also.
So if they change, what is the point of trying to hold on to them, attached to them?
It is like holding water.
It leaks out between your fingers.
When we understand that all things are empty of permanent identity, we do not get caught in the anger or other emotions.
To experience that phenomena are not as substantially established as they initially appear to be, that they are empty of inherent existence, requires deep realization.
With such realization, we don't focus on eliminating our attachments, as is done with a practice that relies primarily on renunciation.
Rather, we understand them as ultimately void of permanence.
The Mahayana view offers the possibility of being engaged in the world, knowing its ultimate nature and yet not being bound by it because we understand emptiness.
Western psychology, which has deeply affected Western culture, has identified three developmental tasks we humans must negotiate in order to mature: attachment, separation, and individuation.
To be psychologically healthy, children must first develop attachment to their parents.
Then later they must separate from them.
And finally, they must develop their own individuality.
Our psychological assumption is that these tasks are essential to becoming fully functioning adults.
Note that these tasks do not include how to relate to the whole as Asian cultures would.
This falls to religion or spiritual practice, and Western religions do teach about our obligations to others.
As we Zen students know, Buddhist teachings emphasize compassion and love for others.
They also encourage us to release, let go of, our fixation on ourselves and on all phenomena.
Non-attachment and the Bodhisattva way are significant aspects of Buddhist teachings.
We Western students are fortunate to have a practice that helps us interrelate while our own culture causes us to individuate.

Although the Eastern origins of Buddhist teachings and language pose some challenges, such as the ones I've listed, to our understanding, there is much we can and do assimilate simply through sitting Zazen, being quiet, and watching the mind.
Plus, when we understand the cultural underpinnings of this Eastern practice we have adopted, we can more easily work with the teachings.
That's the end of my book report.
Thank you.
We have a couple of minutes if anyone has a challenge or a question.
**Participant:** I'm not quite sure.
I really appreciate your enthusiasm for the material.
I felt pretty uncomfortable with a lot of it because it seems so simplistic.
And the argument is really psychologically based.
For example, Uchiyama Roshi says the whole purpose of practice is to grow up and become a mature adult.
Which has everything to do with knowing how to relate and be in relationship.
And that's certainly been my experience of practice.
That's just one example.
I think it's more nuanced than how he lays it out in his book.
I don't know if you experienced it that way also.
That it was a good basic common misunderstandings about what emptiness and attachment and the self is.
But actually it's much more subtle and they're not as much at odds.
At least I haven't experienced them as it sounds like he has and maybe you have.
**Shuko Edie Norton:** I think the book may be better than my version of it.
But I was interested enough to want to talk about it.
I think hearing your experience of how you looked at those concepts and how it came up for you, the validity of them, I'd be really interested to have you sometime and hear about that.
Well, the ones that I mentioned were ideas that I found confusing to me for a number of years in my earlier practice.

And I was interested and gratified to see his bringing the cultural differences into both the psychology and the Western perspective and the Asian perspective, having lived in it as well as been confounded by it.
But even at that, Asian is not a monolith.
The example, he's trained in Theravadan, which is really a Sri Lankan and Indian frame, which is different than Chinese and Japanese.
And Tibetan is different also.
So the kind of cultural norms are somewhat different.
They're not a monolith.
That's true.
And the philosophical system behind Buddhism and the particular flavor of it isn't a monolith either.
Well, I offer one perspective that I enjoyed reading about.
I just want to give a little more fodder for the conversation.
I appreciate that.
Yes?
**Participant:** I appreciate the talk.

I've often had similar thoughts about the veneer of cultural accretion that we carry and that filter that we look through when we try and do something like the religion that we're adopting, essentially, wasn't what we grew up with and certainly wasn't what our parents grew up with.
And we come to it with certain newborn ways of being as Americans and as Westerners that we maybe don't notice, as if we're wearing certain colored glasses.
And sometimes I think that the things that we even sort of get intellectually, we still trip over.
They're almost too close to our experience about how we just view things.
And there were a couple things that you went over there where I was thinking, yeah, that's a real obvious thought, but it's also maybe it's so obvious that I just continually don't think about it.

But the notion that we have these ideas about our identity or our self-worth that are just really wrapped up in the way we have experienced our life here growing up in this country, and we're looking for something.
When we see a religion or something over here that we're going towards, we look at that and we view that through the value system that we're carrying.
Will this help me with my self-worth and help me with the sense of pain that I particularly carry that has to do with my particular psychological angst, my insecurities and whatnot?
And those filters or those attitudes might not be what were applied to that practice in the place it came from, where it came here.
And I kind of look at it as being sort of the way in which Buddhism transforms as it goes from country to country.
We're doing something different here.
We're sort of melding it together with these attitudes we carry.
And somehow magically Buddhism continues to be Buddhism.
**Shuko Edie Norton:** Yes, we don't have much time.
I think we need to stop.
I'm sorry.
Maybe out in the lobby.
